But I also think there is something more fundamental today, which prevents this from being feasible anymore: the systematic destruction of the wisdom respecting self-sufficiency. A lot of people romanticize the idea of living "off grid" or in a way that's "self-sustainable", but the lack of - what used to be called common - sense about the reality of it tends to stagger many people who try, and then you end up with a millennial Jewtube channel depicting self-sustainable living that is anything but.

Living this way doesn't only require certain know-how, it requires a certain mindset and attitude toward life and responsibility. What doesn't get addressed is that every one of these things requires resources to keep alive, cleaning their areas, and a garden (with proper crop cycling) can be fickle. Especially if you are dealing with any amount of property that's 10-15 acres or more, it's a full time job that you can't do during your full time job. Goodbye weekends. That holiday you always take every spring for two weeks? Gonna be tough.

Back in the day, many of the farmsteads hired help from the local community. Sure, it might be possible to do with enough sons. But that makes the community you live in relevant. Helping maintain your property and way of life is going to mean those kids will have to sacrifice participating in a lot of other things "modern" kids do. I grew up in this environment and can remember the kids who couldn't come out for football because they had too much to do after school. Despite being intelligent, they never kept up excellent grades because they would go home and work until dark. The reality is that our modern way of living - the new machine for how we raise kids - just doesn't mesh very well with this old way of doing things. So even socially, you are talking about having to find a very specific kind of community and culture to live within. It isn't an "easy" life, but it sounds poetic to people who haven't done it. And granted, there is a lot of beauty that comes with it. People who love it, love it like life. But there are tradeoffs no doubt.

When I refer to this being impossible for most because of the destruction of wisdom and attitude, it's because most people today just aren't going to be cut out for it. Do they want to have to go outside on a cold autumn night at 11 p.m. because something got into the fenced area, or one of their animals got out, and you've now got to go chase down something that wants nothing to do with you? How about cleaning shit out of places weekly? Clearing snow and plowing a driveway? Cutting firewood and preparing for winter through the summer months? Always be thinking ahead to the next season? Be willing to learn small engines and to maintain that kind of equipment...because this work will require it and the rule is that shit likes to break.

Location itself tends to be a limiting factor. Most people today are used to have amenities like hospitals and stores only 5 or 10 minutes from their homes. Living like the OP suggests implies rural living. Where I grew up you were 35-45 minutes (depending on what direction) from the nearest stores, and hospitals. That means having to have some wisdom when it comes to treating wounds. It means you can't cook a meal you decide to cook 5 minutes in advance. You will inevitably learn some food preservation, but you'll need to get used to eating according to a plan unless you think you're going to drive into town every day.

The other obvious point is that most rural areas are limited in their police force. The counterbalance is that there is less crime generally. But it also means that if shit does hit the fan, you aren't going to have a cop on the corner. You will need to get very comfortable protecting your own home.

I think this way of life is great, and people were probably better off on the whole when it was lived this way more frequently. But I also think humans have been domesticated in ways they don't even appreciate, and a lot of that old attitude toward life has been bred out of people.
